questions.q: What does the target profile set by `qsharp.init(target_profile=...)` control?
options: The color scheme of the Jupyter notebook
The number of shots run per experiment
The Azure region jobs are submitted to
Which subset of Q# language features and gate sets you're compiling against -- restrictive hardware-oriented profiles support less than the permissive default simulator-oriented profile
questions.explain: The target profile determines what Q# features/gates are valid to compile against; a restrictive profile matching real hardware constraints allows less than the default profile, so code valid under one may not compile under the other.

questions.q: Why would you prefer `qsharp.run("Op()", shots=1000)` over a Python for-loop calling `qsharp.eval(...)` 1000 times?
options: qsharp.run performs the repeated sampling natively in one call, which is faster and more idiomatic than looping calls into the Q# runtime from Python one at a time
qsharp.eval cannot be called more than once per session
qsharp.run does not return any results at all
There is no difference between the two approaches
questions.explain: qsharp.run(shots=N) does native repeated sampling in a single call, avoiding the overhead of calling back into the runtime from a Python loop for each shot.

questions.q: What does `qsharp.estimate("MyAlgorithm()")` give you, and why is it useful to call from the same Python session as your development loop?
options: A structured resource-estimate report (physical qubits, runtime, etc.) that you can generate and compare alongside correctness checks in the same notebook/script, without switching to the CLI
It returns the algorithm's measurement histogram instead of an estimate
It submits the algorithm directly to real quantum hardware
It has no practical use and is purely illustrative
questions.explain: qsharp.estimate produces the same kind of resource-estimate report covered in Chapter 3, but callable directly from Python, letting you fold feasibility checks into the same development session as correctness testing.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the `qsharp` package and the `azure-quantum` package in this workflow?
options: qsharp can only be used for resource estimation, never for simulation
They are competing, incompatible packages that cannot be used together
qsharp handles local compilation, simulation, and estimation; azure-quantum handles connecting to a real workspace and submitting the same compiled program to cloud targets
azure-quantum replaces the need for qsharp entirely
questions.explain: qsharp covers local development (compiling, running, estimating); azure-quantum's Workspace/submit() covers taking that same compiled program to a real Azure Quantum workspace target -- complementary, not competing.

questions.q: Why is it more valuable to catch a target-profile compilation mismatch locally than to discover it after a real job submission fails?
options: Local compilation errors are always wrong and should be ignored
There is no actual benefit either way

Catching it locally during development avoids wasted job-queue time and avoids any cost that a real hardware job submission could accrue, compared to discovering the same mismatch only after submitting
Real job failures provide better debugging information than local compilation errors
questions.explain: As covered in Chapter 3, real hardware jobs can queue and accrue cost; catching a profile mismatch locally during compilation avoids wasting that time and money on a job that was never going to succeed.
